newsitem.title: USA: Sidelined Fed seen boosting U.S. earnings outlook.
newsitem.headline: Sidelined Fed seen boosting U.S. earnings outlook.

text.p: Prospects that the Federal Reserve will keep interest rates in check could lead bullish Wall Street analysts to boost their forecasts for U.S. corporate earnings in the second half of the year.

Earnings estimate hikes would be further support to the surging U.S. stock market, which previously expected the Fed to boost rates several times in the second half of the year, cooling the economy and corporate profits, analysts said.

Second-quarter operating earnings are up a better-than-expected 11.3 percent for the two-thirds of the Standard and Poor's 500 companies that have reported thus far, according to First Call, which tracks analyst estimates and earnings.
Some analysts caution that interest rate hikes could still be in the cards, creating a challenge to second-half profits and the overall stock market.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony this week to Congress left Wall Street with the view that monetary policy will remain on hold, at least for the near term.
"I think over the next month we're going to see a general lifting of forward estimates," said Peter Canelo, U.S. equity strategist at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter.

Growth in S&P 500 profits could be closer to 10 percent in the third and fourth quarters, up from Morgan Stanley's previous forecasts of 8.8 percent growth in the third quarter and 7.0 percent in the fourth, Canelo said.
But David Shulman, chief equity strategist at Salomon Brothers, said he did not expect a rash of raised estimates in reaction to perceived Fed policy.
While the Fed may be on hold at its next policy-making meeting in August, Shulman said he still expects rate increases to come.
"We don't expect them to go in August, which is what we previously thought, but September is certainly not out of the question," he said.

Through Wednesday, 322 of the Standard & Poor's 500 companies had reported second-quarter earnings. Of them, 197, or 61 percent, beat Wall Street analysts' consensus earnings expectations, according to research firm I/B/E/S.
Seventy-two, or 22 percent, posted numbers below expectations, while 53, or 16 percent, matched targets.
"On the earnings front there's no problem at all as far as the market is concerned," said Arun Kumar, senior U.S. equities strategist at Lehman Brothers.

Chuck Hill, director of research at First Call, said he expected the S&P 500 earnings to end the second quarter with a rise of 11 percent to 12 percent over 1996's second quarter, topping the 8.9 percent forecast at the outset of the reporting period but shaved down from an earlier 9.5 percent forecast.
Shulman, however, put second-quarter S&P 500 profit growth closer to 8 percent.
Reflecting the benefits of the bull market, the securities industry has put in the strongest second-quarter earnings performance ever, according to Joseph Abbott, assistant vice president at I/B/E/S.

Earnings for companies in the securities industry group came in on average 21 percent above forecasts, Abbott said. Computer networking companies were also robust, reporting profits 13 percent above forecasts.
Laggards included the electric utility group, which posted earnings on average 7 percent below forecasts, hurt by milder-than-normal weather and higher maintenance costs, Abbott said.
Analysts said companies will have to continue to deliver strong earnings in coming quarters for the stock market to maintain its lofty levels.

"The critical variable in watching the market over the next several quarters will be earnings," said Charlie Crane, chief market strategist at Key Asset Management. "If you don't get earnings to support valuations, even if interest rates continue to trend downward, the market could be vulnerable."
